title: Annapurna's open kitchen
hookLine: Shiva calls the world an illusion, food and all, so Parvati vanishes, and the kitchens of the world go empty
carry: food is the goddess's gift, so offer it first
last: PARVATI: IT WAS SHIVA ALL ALONG.

cards: On Kailash, an argument. Shiva, the great ascetic, is explaining that the world of things is illusion, maya: bodies, houses, possessions, even food, none of it ultimately real. Parvati listens.
Then, in the story people tell, she decides to let him find out what that means. She disappears, and with her goes every grain, every loaf, every pot on every stove. The fields stand empty.
Creatures go hungry. Even the gods grow faint. Even Shiva.
Today, Parvati again, and an argument made without a single word.

teach.h: A KITCHEN STILL OPEN IN KASHI.
teach.b: Word comes that somewhere food is still being served. In Kashi, the holy city of Varanasi, a kitchen is open, and at its door stands a goddess with a ladle and a pot that never runs out, feeding everyone who comes.

teach.h: ANNAPURNA, THE ONE FULL OF FOOD.
teach.b: Her name in this story is Annapurna, which tradition explains as the one who is full of food.

teach.h: SHIVA HOLDS OUT A BEGGING BOWL.
teach.b: So Shiva, lord of the universe, the great ascetic who said food was unreal, walks to Kashi with a begging bowl and holds it out to her.

And she fills it. The images of this moment are tender, not triumphant: the goddess serving, the god receiving, a family meal. Some tellers say Shiva learned that the body and its hunger aren't to be waved away.
Some say Parvati wasn't arguing against his teaching at all, but filling it out: in that reading, spirit needs a body to live in, and a body needs to eat.
In Varanasi a temple to Annapurna stands near Shiva's own, and devotees speak of her as the mother who makes sure no one in the city goes hungry. This is why many Hindu homes treat food as holy.
Before eating, a family offers it first, to Annapurna, to Krishna, to the home's deity, and what comes back is prasad, a gift returned.

The old teaching goes deep: in the Taittiriya Upanishad, the seeker Bhrigu's first discovery is that food is Brahman. And with that the five goddesses are met. Tomorrow, the one power moving through them all.

how: Annapurna is honored in homes and kitchens as the goddess of nourishment, and her temple in Varanasi stands near the Kashi Vishwanath temple of Shiva; some families offer a little food to her before a meal.

games.q: you're Shiva. you said food was illusion, and now there's none anywhere, and you're hungry too. word comes of one open kitchen in Kashi. what do you do?

games.why: in the story, Shiva walks to Kashi with a begging bowl, and Annapurna fills it.

practice: Before your next meal, do what many Hindu families do: set a little aside first, or hold the plate still a moment, and offer it. Trace it back while you wait: who cooked it, who carried it, who grew it, the rain, the soil.
Then eat it as a gift returned. If you pray, offer it to Annapurna or God in your own words; if you don't, thank the hands.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The name over all five goddesses met in this run; today, the Goddess as Annapurna, filling Shiva's bowl. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Annapurna; tradition explains the name as 'she who is full of food,' and knows her as a form of Parvati.
